The village is hushed today. Even the gulls are whispering, almost.
My bones say rain by evening. The sky agrees with them, quietly.
A fishing knot lasts longer than a grudge. I tie mine twice.
The pond is flat as a plate today. No wind to stir it.
I watched a dragonfly land on my rod. He stayed a while. Heh.
Old rope and old men both fray slow. That is a comfort.
The heron is preening on the far post. He knows I see him.
A quiet day is good for mending. Nets, and other things.
The tide creeps in like a shy cat. Slow, but it arrives.
My boat sits ready by the reeds. No rush to launch her.
Even the fish seem to doze today. I do not blame them.
A proverb a day keeps the hurry away. Heh. I made that one.
The mist is thin today. The fish can see me thinking.
Sand under my boots remembers every tide. So do my knees.
I counted seven ripples and then lost count. A fine morning.
The kettle whistles at noon. That is the village clock.
A slow cast is a kind of prayer. The pond hears it.
My hat has a hole from that heron's beak. Long story. Heh.
The reeds are green and patient. They outlast the winter.
Bait sits in my tin, waiting. Waiting is most of it.
I saw a turtle cross the path. He was not in a hurry.
The water holds the clouds like a mirror. A wobbly mirror.
Old fishermen talk little. The line does the talking. Heh.
The sun is warm on the dock planks. Good for sitting.
A tangled leader teaches knots. I have learned many times.
The heron and I share the shallows. He takes, I watch.
My pipe is cold today. The mist is enough smoke for me.
Quiet water reflects a quiet mind. Mine is nearly there.
The village cat visits my boat sometimes. He inspects the ropes.
A fish jumped and left a ring. The pond keeps its secrets.
I sharpened my hook this morning. Sharp hooks catch thoughts too. Heh.
The breeze smells of rain and green things. Good signs.
My net hangs in the shed, dry. It dreams of water, maybe.
A slow day is a gift for old bones. I accept it gladly.
The tide book says low water at dusk. I will be here.
The heron coughed at me this morning. A greeting, perhaps.
Sandpipers run the shoreline like they owe it something. Heh.
I watched the mist curl off the pond. It looked like breath.
A knot in the line is better than a knot in the heart. Heh.
My hands smell of bait and salt. Honest smells, both.
The pond has no hurry in it. I try to borrow that.
The far hill is blue with distance. The fish are closer.
An old boat and an old man, both waiting for the tide. Heh.
The heron's shadow crossed my line. He is bold today.
I found a smooth stone on the bank. I kept it for luck.
The water is warm at the edges. The deep stays cold.
A dragonfly rested on my float. The float did not move.
My tea went cold while I watched the reeds. Worth it.
The village is quiet but the pond is quieter. I like that.
A good day for nothing much. Nothing much is enough. Heh.
The heron is fishing the far bank. We respect each other's spots.
I hear the mill wheel turning slow. The stream is low.
My boots are damp from the grass. Morning dew does that.
A fish rose and looked at me. Then he was gone. Heh.
The sky is gray wool today. The pond wears it well.
Old lures in my box tell stories. I let them rest.
The tide will turn when it turns. I will still be here.
A quiet village day is a long, slow cast. I wait for the bite. Heh.
